source.title: Sparse but Wrong: Incorrect L0 Leads to Incorrect Features in Sparse Autoencoders

page_placements.theme: Feature hedging: narrow or too-sparse SAEs mix correlated features into latents

record.tranche_reason: The study varies SAE L0 and measures latent mixing and decoder geometry, providing a different-method test of whether the SAE training objective can produce feature-structure artifacts. It does not test dictionary-size-driven feature splitting.
record.gate_note: The paper studies how incorrect L0 affects feature mixing, not whether increasing dictionary size replaces a coarse feature with finer features that partition its inputs. It does not directly test nested feature families, hierarchical splitting or Matryoshka SAEs. Rows below bear on V6's objective-artifact aspect; the other claim versions are not tested.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps SAE L0 at fixed width and measures whether latents mix correlated features. It does not measure feature splitting: no coarse feature is shown replaced by finer ones as the dictionary grows. Feature splitting appears only as a related-work citation (Bricken et al.; Templeton et al.). The mixing it measures is a related but different construct (feature hedging due to low L0). It belongs under fits_no_version, not V6, because V6 concerns splitting being an objective artifact.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also conclude that sparsity–reconstruction tradeoff plots are misleading, since a correct dictionary reconstructs worse at low L0. They add that most open-source SAEs (L0 below 100) have too low an L0, and that the elbow before cdec rises coincides with peak sparse probing.
record.recipe_differences: The study sweeps SAE L0 and measures decoder cosine geometry and sparse probing, with toy-model ground truth. It does not compare dictionaries of increasing width to test feature splitting.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with L0, correlation sign and strength, SAE family (BatchTopK versus JumpReLU), SAE width, and whether training starts below or above the correct L0. The L0 associated with the cdec minimum differs by model, layer, and SAE family; some curves have broad shallow minima.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed width, an L0 below the true L0 makes nearly every latent absorb positive or negative components of correlated features. MSE rewards this (2.73 vs 4.88 ground truth), and proofs show the disentangled SAE is not a local minimum. Too-high L0 also gives degenerate mixing. In LLMs, decoder pairwise cosine similarity rises sharply at low L0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mis-set SAE sparsity (L0) makes the training objective mix correlated features into latents (feature hedging), an objective artifact distinct from feature splitting.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306 (2026)
record.problems: LLM experiments cover only a few layers and two model families, and the authors say cdec has broad minima in some settings and correlates imperfectly with sparse probing, especially at high L0. Feature mixing in LLMs is inferred from decoder geometry and projection histograms rather than compared with known ground-truth features. Several plotted values are not stated numerically in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Sparse-probing F1 curves are not included as rows because they measure downstream probing performance rather than feature mixing or splitting. Open-source SAE L0 distributions are also omitted because they report the prevalence of L0 values, not a measured feature-structure outcome.

untested.parts: No dictionary-width sweep or coarse-to-fine split analysis.
No splitting test in large models or open SAE releases. Open SAEs are surveyed only for their L0 values.
No parent/child absorption test. Absorption is cited only.
No comparison of latents across SAE sizes.
No measure of splitting itself, and no Matryoshka SAE. The objective-artifact result concerns L0-driven mixing of correlated features, not splitting.

record.verdict_notes: Unrecorded results bear only on the fits_no_version claim, not on any splitting version. These include mixing vs correlation strength and vs L0 (App. D.1-D.2), superposition-noise toy models (D.3, E.1), and narrow-width SAEs combining hedging with L0 mixing (E.2). The reader's V6 link conflated feature mixing/hedging with splitting.

versions.untested_parts: No dictionary-size sweep or test of whether multiple fine features cover a smaller dictionary feature's inputs and lie near its direction.
No scaling of dictionary size or test of splitting across SAE families or open SAE releases.
No nested feature families, concept hierarchy, or test of whether split features partition parent inputs.
No parent-child absorption or firing-coverage test.
No comparison of larger- and smaller-dictionary latents or test for novel latents.

Tests L0-related feature mixing on correlated synthetic data and SAE decoder geometry in LLMs. Does not directly test feature splitting, hierarchical inputs, or whether Matryoshka SAEs change or reduce splitting.

rows.subject: 5-feature toy model
rows.operation_detail: Trained BatchTopK SAEs at L0 values below and equal to the data's true L0.

conditions.value: f0 positively correlated with f1 through f4

rows.measure: Decoder cosine similarity with ground-truth features
rows.baseline: At L0=2, the SAE perfectly learns the underlying true features.
rows.value: At L0=1.8, latents tracking f1 through f4 mix in a positive component of f0.
rows.note: The text describes the mixing pattern; the cosine values themselves are shown in the figure.
rows.check: Measures mixing of a correlated feature f0 into latents at L0 below true L0, not splitting. The mixing itself is clearly observed.

relation.reason: Splitting is cited in one related-work sentence (Bricken, Templeton), next to hedging and absorption. The paper neither tests nor uses splitting.

tranche.reason: Fixed-width L0 sweep on toy models and LLM SAEs, with no comparison across dictionary sizes. Appendix E.2's narrow-width test is about hedging, not splitting. Splitting appears only in related work.

source_check.notes: r5's MSE comparison is from the 50-feature toy model, not the 5-feature one. Its '100k training samples' are evaluation samples for MSE; the SAEs were trained on 15M. The paper shares an author with an original and frames its result as feature hedging due to low L0. It touches V6 only loosely: the objective causes mixing, and splitting is not measured.

statements.correction: Toy models at fixed width (h=g): with SAE L0 below true L0, nearly all latents mix in positive components of positively correlated features and negative components of anti-correlated ones. The authors call this feature hedging, not absorption. 50-feature model (true L0 11), SAE L0=5: trained SAE MSE 2.73 vs 4.88 for the ground-truth SAE. Theorem F.2: the disentangled SAE is not a local minimum when L0 is below true L0. At L0=18, solutions are degenerate and mixed, but many latents stay correct.
statements.problem: Numbers and claims are right: 2.73 vs 4.88 (L0=5, 50-feature toy model), Theorems F.1/F.2, and degenerate solutions at too-high L0. 'Nearly every latent' matches the intro's 'nearly all latents'. But 'absorbs' risks being read as feature absorption (V4). The paper calls this mixing/feature hedging and contrasts it with absorption, which needs very high correlation.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Correlated toy-model inputs with incorrect L0
reader_labels.reason: The low-L0 SAEs mix correlated feature components, and the text reports that high L0 can also produce mixed or degenerate features (r1-r5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: LLM SAEs and changing L0 during training
reader_labels.reason: Decoder geometry indicates a low-L0 mixing regime, but minima can be broad, outcomes differ across SAE families and settings, and starting too low leaves persistent errors (r6-r12, r17).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The high-L0 condition at 750 has both a narrower central distribution and a large positive hump, which the authors interpret as mixed behavior across latents rather than a uniform effect (r13-r16).
